Copper-Catalyzed Stereoselective Defluoroalkylation or
-arylation of gem-Difluoroallenes To Form
Monofluoroallenes under Mild Conditions
Yaoming Tan
+

[a]
Kailun Chen
+
,
[a]
Jiaxin Hu,
[a]
Sen Lin,
[a]
and Tao Wu*
[a, b]
Herein, we demonstrate the formation of monofluoroallenes
through copper-catalyzed defluoroalkylation or defluoroaryla-
tion of gem-difluoroallenes using affordable and readily avail-
able Grignard reagents. Additionally, alkyl lithium or alkyl zinc
reagents proved successful in these transformations. Under
mild conditions, monofluoroallenes can be converted into
fluorinated olefinic compounds or non-fluorinated alkyne
compounds. Initial mechanistic studies suggest that the reac-
tion may start with an organocopper reagent and undergo a
rapid β-F elimination step. Although the current enantiomeric
excess is low, chiral ligands could facilitate the asymmetric
transformation of this reaction.
Introduction
The incorporation of a fluorine atom in an organic molecule can
lead to substantially altered properties, including biological
activity, physical and chemical parameters, as well as material
performances, as compared to a non-fluorinated compound.
[1]
Significant progress has been made in the synthesis of alkyl,
alkenyl, aryl, or acyl C � F bonds,
[2]
but the development of
compounds containing allenyl C � F bonds is still in its infancy,
perhaps due to concerns about the stability of such species.
[3]
Due to its promising conversion capability based on allenyl
functional groups,
[4]
monofluoroallene can serve as a single
building block for the synthesis of C � F compounds bearing
alkyl, alkenyl, alkynyl, carbonyl, carboxylic acids, and other
valuable functional groups. Consequently, the development of
simple and efficient methods to construct allenyl fluorides is of
synthetic importance. Furthermore, as allenyl groups become
more prevalent as crucial building blocks in numerous drug
molecules, organic ligands, and materials chemistry molecules,
[5]
this novel fluorinated allenyl moiety provides new opportunities
for molecular design and editing in these fields.
Hayashi
[6]
and Toste
[7]
independently reported the metal-
catalyzed defluoroalkylation and defluorosilylation of propargyl
gem-difluorides to monofluoroalkenes (Scheme 1A top). Our
group also discovered the nickel-catalyzed defluorination of
iodoallyl gem-difluorides under reducing conditions to obtain
allenyl monofluorides (Scheme 1A bottom).
[8]
In these reactions,
alkenyl metal species serve as central intermediates, whose β-F
elimination produces the ultimate monofluorinated product.
Hammond and co-workers presented an alternative precursor,
gem-difluoroallenes, that facilitated the production of mono-
fluoroallenes through their defluorinated nucleophilic substitu-
tion reaction. However, this process necessitated a significant
excess of copper salts and only two examples have been
reported.
[9]
Inspired by the currently extensively studied cata-
lytic defluorinative functionalization reactions of gem-
difluoroalkenes,
[10]
we are attempting to implement a catalytic
version of the Hammond’s strategy and explore the substrate
range and asymmetric trials of the method. We hereby report
on the synthesis of monofluoroallenes upon a copper-catalyzed

Results and Discussion
We began our hypothesis with gem-difluoroallenes 1 a and
EtMgBr 2 a under metal catalysts (Table 1). The optimal
conditions were finally obtained by systematic examination of
the metal catalyst, ligand, base and other reaction parameters
such as temperature, solvent, and time, providing the desired
monofluoroallene 3 a in 99 % GC yield and 88 % isolated yield
(entry 1). Control experiments showed that copper catalysts
played important roles in the reactions. Other metal catalysts,
such as palladium or nickel, were ineffective in this trans-
formation (entries 2 and 3). Copper catalysts, other than CuCl,
could also catalyze this reaction, but with less efficiently
(entries 4 and 5). Notably, 3 a was also obtained using copper(II)
salt catalysts (entry 6). Adding a ligand is not advantageous to
the reaction and diminishes the yield (entries 7 and 8). The low
temperatures slowed down the reactions and gave a decreased
yield (entries 9 and 10). Solvents were proven to be one of the
most important factors affecting the reactions. Toluene or
Hexane, instead of THF as the solvent, would drastically
decrease the yield and give 3 a with 10 % or 27 % GC yield
respectively (entries 11 and 12). The amount of Grignard
reagent used was another critical factor affecting the efficiency
of the conversion. Excessive amounts of EtMgBr probably would
cause further conversion of the product of 3 a (entry 13). Lower
catalyst loading would consequently lead to lower yield of
desire monoallenyl fluoride and a significant amount of 1 a was
recovered (entry 14). The removal of copper metal completely
shut down the reaction (entry 15).
With an optimal process in hand, we next investigated the
scope of the gem-difluoroallenes component in this trans-
formation (Scheme 2). Various trisubstituted monofluoroallenes
were smoothly obtained with satisfactory yields by the
combination of corresponding allenes 4 and EtMgBr in the
presence of the copper catalyst. A wide array of substituted
phenylethyl difluoroallenes, bearing methyl at the ortho-, meta-,
and para-positions, or electron donating group-OMe, or elec-
tron withdrawing group-CF
3
, or halide group at the para-
positions, worked well, affording expected defluoroethylation
allenes 5 b–5 i in good to excellent yields. Noteworthy, bromo-
and chloro-substrates 4 c and 4 g, which were easily coupled
with Grignard regents under transition metal catalysts, were
tolerated and retained under our reaction conditions, trans-
ferring to ethylated allenes 5 c and 5 g in 70 % and 68 % yields
respectively. Phenyl and dimethyl substituted phenylethyl
allenes were also applied to reaction conditions and to furnish
the desired products 5 j, 5 k and 5 m in moderate to excellent
yields. Pyridine or thiophene tethered allenes 4 n and 4 o
engaged in the reactions, and successfully defluorinated and
alkylation to furnish the corresponding allenyl fluorides 5 n and
5 o in moderate yields. Benzylated gem-difluoroallenes, also
worked well and afford 5 p and 5 q in contented yields. 1-
cyclohexylethylated, 1-cyclohexylmethylated, cyclohexylated al-
lenes, a series of substrates accompanied by decreasing carbon
chains, were tested, and gently transferred to anticipated
products 5 r–5 t in good yields. Prolonged carbon chain
monofluoroallene 5 u was also achieved at 70 % yield. Racemic
substrate 4 v with a tertiary carbon, afforded two unseparatable
diastereoisomers at 84 % yield with 1.6 : 1 dr, which was
attributed to generation of the axial chirality of allenes via
defluoroalkylation process. It is gratifying to note that tetrasub-

reaction conditions and defluoroalkylation product 5 w, persub-
stituted monofluoroallene was acquired with 81 % yield.
We next investigated different Grignard reagents displaying
a variety of electronic and steric properties (Scheme 3). All types
of alkyl Grignard reagents could be used to afford the
corresponding defluoroalkylation monofluoroallenes in moder-
ate or excellent yields. Long carbon chain Grignard species,
tetradecylmagnesium chloride, smoothly reacted with gem-
difluoroallenes 1 a, and tetradecylated desired product 7 d was
afforded at 51 % yield. Other commercial alkyl magnesium
compounds, such as iso-propyl, iso-butyl, and tert-butyl, also
worked well in these transformations, leading to allenes 7 e–7 g
respectively. A cyclopropyl group also could be introduced into
monofluoroallene 7 h with related metal species, in which ring-
opening products were not detected. Acetal-protected carbonyl
containing Grignard compound, 6 k engaged in the reaction
and was transferred to allenyl fluoride 7 k in 67 % yield, easy to
remove the protecting group and return to the aldehyde group
for more relevant transformations. Aryl magnesium bromides or
chlorides, were also examined in this process. Moderated yields
of defluoroarylated allenes 7 l–7 o were achieved under low
temperature, stemmed from the low stability of these aryl-
allenyl fluorides. Other metal species, also were considered and
applied into this system. Organozinc reagents, and organo-
lithium compounds, were participated in the reaction instead of
Grignard reagents and the corresponding products were
obtained, nevertheless with less efficiency.
Because of the rich reactivity of the allene group, we expect
that these monofluoroallenes products could be converted into
more useful synthons (Scheme 4). First, it is simple to expand
our reactions to 1 mmol scale, just with a little lower yield of
product 3 a. Second, alkynes compounds can be obtained
simply by tandem reactions from 1 a. Alkyne 8 was afforded by
addition of PhMgBr into the mixture of our reaction without the
separation of monofluoroallene 3 a.
[12]
It is a new way to
synthesis kinds of alkynes by simple operation of changing
substitutes on gem-difluoroallenes and Grignard reagents.
Allenyl fluoride 3 a, a new sp
2
C � F bond compound, was
transferred to alkyl fluoride 9 by palladium-catalyzed hydro-
genation at atmospheric pressure and room temperature with
85 % yield,
[13]
in which C � F bond was retained.
We designed several controlled experiments to try to
explore the mechanism of the reaction (Scheme 5). 1 a was
almost completely recovered in the absence of copper
catalyst.
[14]
After mixing the substrates 1 a and 2 a with 0.5
equivalent copper salt for one hour, the reaction was quenched
by adding saturated aqueous ammonium chloride solution or
benzaldehyde respectively.
[15]
Expected allyl gem-difluoride 11
and allyl alcohol 12 were not detected when analyzing of the
residues of the above quenched reactions, other than 72 % yield
of 3 a was obtained.
[16]
These results seem to imply that the
reaction proceeds through the alkyl copper species and gives
the final product by its speedy β-F elimination via an alkenyl
copper intermediate.
[17]
We also tried asymmetric reactions,
although moderate enantioselectivity could be obtained, but
the conversion of this reaction was low.

Conclusions
We have developed a copper-catalyzed synthesis of monofluor-
oallenes via defluorination of gem-difluoroallenes under mild
conditions. This procedure generated various alkylated or
arylated allenyl monofluorides with moderate to excellent yield
using commercial Grignard reagents. Other metal species,
including organozinc and organolithium compounds, can also
be used with these new catalytic approaches. Monoallenyl
fluorides are crucial precursors for organic synthesis as they can
be easily converted to alkynes or alkyl fluorides by a simple
process. Mechanistic studies have indicated that the reaction
may involve organocopper species and alkenyl copper inter-
mediates, resulting in the desired products through β-F
elimination. Although attempts at inducing asymmetric reac-
tions with chiral ligands were unsuccessful, they are currently
the focus of our ongoing research.
Experimental Section
To an oven-dried tube equipped with a magnetic stir bar, CuCl
(2 mg, 0.02 mmol) and THF (0.8 mL) were added and cooled
to� 60 ° C under nitrogen. Subsequently, Grignard reagent 2 a or 6
(1.1 equiv, 0.22 mmol) was added and stirred for 5 minutes at this
temperature. Then, a THF solution of allene 1 a or 4 (1 mL,
0.2 mmol/1 mL, 1 equiv) was added. The cold bath was removed,
and the reaction was stirred at room temperature for 5 hours. The
reaction was quenched with methanol and saturated NH
4
Cl
aqueous solution at 0 ° C, and purified by silica gel column
chromatography to afford the desired products.
